searchText: Just thinking out loud: how about something akin to sequencer auctions? Data availability providers bid for slots, put up a bond, are slashed for inactivity / signing invalid data. Fees earned from validiums/volitions and exiting users. Proving data availability is hard. IPFS actually did solve it for certain classes of data availability. And the Ethereum R&D teams are in theory trying to solve a similar problem with proof of execution. Does increasing block size + economic incentives for nodes to serve each other data count? Like in arweave https://www.arweave.org/yellow-paper.pdf No, that doesn't give any guarantees that data is actually available on the network. It just increases the probability that once the data is available it will stay available. okay yes, this is after validators agree to keep it available but bigger blocks and instead of altruism there's incentives bigger blocks increase the hardware and network requirements to run nodes, meaning fewer people will run them overall There exists a happy space where there's enough capacity for lots of interesting L2s without significantly impacting the average users ability to run a node yes but you only need to trust 1 of N to serve data and with incentives even that one person doesnt have to be altrusitic increasing block size drives N down much more than the inventives to profit off serving data would drive it up No, anyone can submit a transaction/block that is missing data. The data availability problem is that you can't tell when someone didn't share data with the network. Well, there are two data availability problems and that is one of them. The other is that data that used to be available on the network no longer is. That one tends to be a tad easier to mitigate though. Yup I guess I'm discussing this So there would be an equilibrium, I'm guessing its higher blocksize than ethereum today I'm guessing it's not since it's *already* a decent amount of work to run a node, although hopefully that decreases with better pruning functionality nodes are paid zero to serve data today though incentives for nodes havent been seriously tried on ethereum because blocksize so small they were never needed other chains have tried is there any other projects trying what you're describing? arweave Ethereum solved the data availability problem with forking. The same solution doesn't work on L2s because they can't fork. If you don't have access to a block body, you'll fork away (as will everyone else) so not supplying the data to the network will result in everyone essentially ignoring your block. I'll read this over later, a little busy rn Sorry, maybe I should clarify. solution im suggesting is: L2 (sequencer) pushes data to L1, majority of L1 validators agree then its on-chain, then they send to nodes difference is instead of nodes being altruistic, now they pay each other to get data from each other but the point I'm getting at is that the rule of thumb that's served decentralized systems for a while now is that many small nodes is better than a few large nodes, even if the large nodes have incentives to keep them well behaved, as the latter (which large blocks encourage) can lead to corruption > majority of L1 validators agree then its on-chain It isn't L2 anymore if L1 has to do work to verify it. It is just L1. Well yes Just suggesting how to increase amount of data L1 can keep available Oh okay, why? And P.S. If thats true maybe its a theoretical limit, each node has x dollars they want to altruistically burn, once youve consumed all that in storage costs then only way out is everyone doesnt store everything one way out of that is with something like a regenesis where you have periodic checkpoints where you throw away all the old blocks and just keep the historical headers, meaning that new nodes only need to sync from the last regenesis checkpoint maybe its worth trying to plot a graph of idk, x (dollars willing to burn altruistically) versus N (number of nodes willing to burn that) you don't have a lot of ever growing storage that needs to be stored forever it *does* make some sense to have an incentivization structure for that very old deep state > x (dollars willing to burn altruistically) not sure if this is the right model to analyze it, as it's not purely altruistically every user has an interest in promoting decentralization of the network and fending off dos attacks on it and if running a node is easy and lightweight on peoples devices, then taking into consideration "sticky defaults" many users will be able to run nodes without taking conscious action to if their wallets do it for them if this is private loss public good then worth counting under altruism? "*someone* should be doing this for the good of the network but I dont personally want to be the one doing it" so I guess that's saying if x is small N is very large, idk if it makes my model wrong I don't think it's *pure* altruism, since if the user has value in the network they *do* have a rational self interest to promote decentralization as long as there's one other node doing it, no need for you to its public good problem haha well no, as with only one other node (or a small number of nodes) then that makes the network very weak and prone to corruption well yes, rational strategy for a game with public good is often such that the public good doesnt end up happening if not for a few altruistic actors that's true
